body:
A used vape is not ordinary trash. It contains a lithium battery, electronics, plastics and residual liquid containing nicotine, and each of those needs different handling. Throwing a device in the household bin or the curbside recycling can start fires in garbage trucks and recycling plants, and leaking liquid is hazardous to children, pets and the environment. This guide explains why disposal matters, why not to use household trash or curbside recycling, where to take vapes and batteries, how to prepare a device for drop-off, what to do with liquids, pods and coils, how to deal with damaged devices and how to reduce waste in the first place. It is general information for adults aged 21 and over, and local rules differ, so check yours. Nicotine is addictive.

## Why it matters
Lithium batteries can start fires when they are crushed or punctured, which can happen in garbage trucks, compactors and recycling plants. Such fires are a real risk to workers and facilities, and they are a reason many municipalities have specific rules. Nicotine liquid is hazardous to children, pets and wildlife if it leaks, and it should not enter drains or soil. Devices also contain metals and plastics that can be recovered when they are recycled properly. Responsible disposal is part of being an adult user.

## Do not put them in household trash or curbside recycling
Many municipalities treat vapes as electronic or hazardous waste, and put them on the list of items that must not go in household bins. Even where rules are relaxed, a lithium battery in a bin is a fire risk. Check your local rules on your city or county waste page, and follow them. If you are unsure, treat the device as hazardous waste.

## Where to take them
- **Household hazardous waste sites** and collection events, which accept batteries, electronics and liquids.
- **Electronics recycling programs** that accept small electronics, including some retail take-back programs.
- **Battery drop-off locations** at some retailers, which may accept lithium batteries, sometimes only certain types or sizes.
- **Municipal collection days** for bulky or electronic waste.

Search for your city's hazardous waste page, or use a recycling locator that lets you search by item and location. Call ahead if you are unsure whether a site accepts vapes, because acceptance varies.

## Before you drop it off
Stop using any damaged or swollen device. Put it in a sealed plastic bag, tape over any exposed battery terminals, and keep it away from heat and flammable items. Do not try to open, crush or puncture it, and do not try to remove the battery from a disposable. Keep it out of reach of children and pets until you can take it. If the device is leaking, double-bag it, wear gloves and wash your hands afterward.

### Small steps that reduce risk
- Store used devices in a cool, dry place in a container, not loose in a drawer.
- Do not stack many devices together with exposed terminals.
- Take devices for recycling promptly, instead of letting them build up.

## Liquids
Do not pour leftover liquid down the drain or onto the ground. Absorb small amounts with cat litter or paper towels, seal in a bag and take it to hazardous waste, following local guidance. For unused bottles you no longer want, ask your hazardous waste site what they accept. Keep bottles capped and out of reach of children and pets until you can take them, as explained in [keeping vapes and e-liquid away from children and pets](/blog/keeping-vapes-away-from-children-and-pets/).

## Pods and coils
Used pods and coils go in the same stream as the device, unless your local program says otherwise. They contain residue, and some contain small metal parts. Collect them in a sealed bag and take them with your device. Do not rinse them down the sink.

## Nicotine pouches
Used pouches are small, but they still contain nicotine residue and should not be left where children or pets can reach them. Dispose of them in a bin with a lid, or follow local guidance. Empty cans are usually recyclable where your local program accepts that kind of container, but check the rules. See [how to store nicotine pouches](/blog/how-to-store-nicotine-pouches/).

## Packaging
Cartons and padding from your order are ordinary materials and can usually go in recycling. Remove address labels if you prefer. Keep any original packaging for a short while if you might return an item. See [discreet packaging](/blog/discreet-packaging-what-to-expect/).

## Reducing waste
- **Choose rechargeable devices** that you can use for longer, and consider refillable systems if they suit you.
- **Match the product to your use,** so you do not throw away large amounts of unused product.
- **Avoid stockpiling** more than you will use, because old products can degrade.
- **Take devices for recycling** instead of throwing them away.
- **Buy replacement parts** such as pods and coils instead of replacing a whole device, where your device supports it.

See [rechargeable vs non-rechargeable disposables](/blog/rechargeable-vs-non-rechargeable-disposables/) and [how to pick replacement coils and pods](/blog/how-to-pick-replacement-coils-and-pods/).

## What if there is a fire or smoke?
If a battery smokes, gets very hot or catches fire, do not touch it with bare hands. If it is possible to do so without risk, move flammable items away, and call emergency services. Keep people and pets away. Afterward, treat the device as hazardous waste. See [lithium battery care basics](/blog/lithium-battery-care-basics-for-vapes/).

## Frequently asked questions in depth
### Can I put a vape in the regular bin if there is no recycling nearby?
It is not recommended, because of the fire risk. Look for the nearest hazardous waste site, or ask your city about collection options.

### Can I mail a used vape back to you?
We do not accept used devices through the returns process. Our returns policy covers unopened items. Dispose of used devices locally.

### What about empty bottles?
Empty bottles still contain residue. Check with your local hazardous waste program, and keep them out of reach until you dispose of them.

### Are disposables recyclable?
The battery and electronics can be recycled at the right facility. The device as a whole should go to electronics or hazardous waste recycling, not household recycling.

### How do I find a recycling site?
Search your city or county's waste page, or use a recycling locator for electronics and batteries.

## Related
Learn about [battery care](/blog/lithium-battery-care-basics-for-vapes/) and [keeping vapes away from children and pets](/blog/keeping-vapes-away-from-children-and-pets/). Browse [disposable vapes](/shop/disposables/). All products are for adults aged 21 and over, and nicotine is addictive.

## A worked example: clearing out a drawer
You find five finished disposables in a drawer, two with scuffed casings. You put on gloves, check that none is swollen or hot, and place them in a sealed plastic bag, with tape over the charging ports of the scuffed ones. You search your city's website for "household hazardous waste", find a drop-off site that accepts small electronics and batteries and note its hours. You also gather two empty bottles and a used pod, bag them separately and bring everything on Saturday morning. At the site, you tell the attendant what you have, and they take it. The whole task takes less than an hour, and the drawer is clear.

## Common mistakes
- **Putting devices in the bin** because they look like plastic.
- **Leaving finished devices lying around,** where children or pets might find them.
- **Crushing or opening a device** to remove the battery.
- **Pouring liquid down the sink.**
- **Stacking devices together** with exposed terminals.

Avoiding these keeps you, your household and waste workers out of harm's way. If you make one of them by mistake, move the item to a hard surface away from flammable items, and call your local waste authority for advice.

## A note for retailers
If you run a shop, you may have additional obligations for handling and disposing of returned or expired stock. Check with your local authorities and a licensed waste handler. Do not mix vapor products with general trade waste.

## Frequently asked questions in depth
### Can I bring many devices at once?
Many sites accept household quantities. If you have a large number, call first, because there may be limits per visit.

### Do I have to remove the battery?
No, and you should not try. Take the whole device. Removing a battery from a sealed device can damage it and cause a fire.

### Is there a cost?
Many household hazardous waste programs are free for residents. Retail take-back programs are often free too. Check with the site.

### What if I cannot find a site nearby?
Contact your city or county waste department, or ask a local electronics retailer. Until you can take the items, store them in a sealed bag in a cool place, out of reach of children and pets.

## Planning disposal as part of your routine
The easiest way to dispose of devices responsibly is to make it a routine instead of a chore. Keep a small lidded container in a high place for finished devices and pods. When it is half full, take it to a drop-off site on a day when you are already out, such as when you shop or run errands. Note the dates of local collection events on a calendar. If you live with other adults who use these products, agree who takes the container. A routine means that finished devices never pile up, and that nothing is left lying around.

## Why it is worth the effort
Each device you recycle keeps a lithium battery out of the waste stream and returns materials to use. It also keeps nicotine residue away from children, pets and water. The effort is small compared with the risk of a fire in a bin or a collection truck, and compared with the harm a leaking bottle can do. Responsible disposal is one of the simplest ways to be a considerate adult user.

### What the process looks like at a drop-off site
You arrive, tell an attendant what you have and hand over the sealed bag or place it where they direct. The attendant sorts it into the correct stream. You do not need to explain how you used it, and you are not judged for using it. The aim is to get the items out of circulation securely and responsibly.

faq.q: Can I throw a vape in the trash?
faq.a: No. A vape contains a lithium battery, electronics and nicotine residue. Take it to hazardous waste or electronics recycling.

faq.q: Where can I take used vapes?
faq.a: Household hazardous waste sites and events, electronics recycling programs and some battery drop-off locations. Check your local rules.

faq.q: How should I prepare a device for drop-off?
faq.a: Put it in a sealed bag, tape over exposed terminals, keep it away from heat and do not open or crush it.

faq.q: What do I do with leftover liquid?
faq.a: Do not pour it down the drain. Absorb small amounts with cat litter or paper towels, seal in a bag and take it to hazardous waste.

faq.q: What about used pods and coils?
faq.a: They go in the same stream as the device unless your local program says otherwise.

faq.q: Can I return used devices to you?
faq.a: No. Our returns policy covers unopened items only. Dispose of used devices locally.
